editorial:
J'accuse! (1919) is a French silent anti-war epic written and directed by Abel Gance, produced by PathÃ© FrÃ¨res and first screened in Paris on 25 April 1919. Gance filmed portions of the picture on actual WWI battlefields and recruited real soldiers â€” many of whom perished at Verdun within weeks of shooting â€” for the celebrated 'return of the dead' finale, giving the film a documentary force unmatched in its era. PathÃ© Exchange Inc. handled US theatrical distribution. For a creator today, the 1919 photographic print is fully free in the United States: the maximum 95-year copyright term expired in 2014, and any URAA restoration of a lapsed US registration would have been subject to the same ceiling and expired by the same date.

The live rights trap is the 2007 commercial restoration by Lobster Films and Nederlands Filmmuseum, released on DVD and DCP by Flicker Alley with a newly commissioned symphonic score by Robert Israel. Both the restoration print (reflecting original editorial choices in combining six source elements) and Israel's score are independently copyrighted works. A creator who downloads a file derived from the Flicker Alley release is not working with a free work, even though the underlying 1919 images are public domain. Archive.org hosts multiple copies of the film; those not sourced from the Flicker Alley restoration are the appropriate starting point.
faq: Can I freely copy or adapt footage from J'accuse! (1919)?

Yes, if you use a copy of the original 1919 print â€” the photographic images are in the public domain in the United States, the 95-year term having expired in 2014. If the copy you are using comes from the 2007 Flicker Alley/Lobster Films restoration, that specific print and Robert Israel's score are separately protected. Use an Archive.org upload that is not derived from the Flicker Alley release to stay in the clear.
Does URAA complicate the US public-domain status of this French film?

Potentially in theory, not in practice. Abel Gance died in 1981, so French copyright runs to 2051, and the film was still protected in France when URAA took effect in 1996. If the original US registration lapsed from non-renewal in 1946â€“1947, URAA section 104A may have restored that US copyright at the time. But even a restored URAA term is capped at 95 years from the 1919 publication date, placing its expiry in 2014. The URAA question is historically interesting but has no practical effect on reuse today.
